And the youth grass and worked the house teacher center for that. I don't know, it's been so long. Because it wasn't happening on the court. It was at the middle.
Well did you have any favorite musicians for playing funeral marches in those days? Who were some of your favorite men in the street for playing funeral marches in olden times?
My favorite men. Men, well I used to play with all of them. The favorite men was the men in the excessive man. The men in the tuxedo, the men in the onward band. And the men in the touring.

But say who you remember would be especially good playing a baritone solo in those days? Was there anybody who specialized in something like Wes Lawn Derridge? Oh, John Porter. John Porter, huh? Yeah. John Porter, huh? Who did he work with?

Oh, with the tuxedo man. Playing the baritone solo. John Porter, the one of the back-to-one man. And bass man too. He could play saxophone. He played tennis. Right. That reminds me, what did Davy Jones play in the street?
Alto sax. Alto sax in the street. He could play them all those days too. I thought he played some other instrument. He played acorns. He could play that. Where was he from?
David Jones was from, uh, in the street. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. He played acorns.
He could play that. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Where was he from? David Jones was from, um… right up there where John Porter came from. Up the river… Up the river… Neilera Plaza…
Yeah, Oakland Plaza… Yeah, Oakland Plaza…
Yeah, up around there. They were all boys together.
A lot here or someplace like that? Yeah, around the lot here I think. Yeah, they were. But he traveled around with big bands, don't you say?
Oh yeah, him and John told us they'd been all over.
Well what kind of bands were they? Were they dance bands, regular orchestras, or were they dance bands?

Well David Jones was regular orchestras, but John Poulter and Percy Humphrey Dad, and another other place they used to call Davis. Do you know him? No I don't know him. They had old Rupert's. They used to play in them shoes. Like Ring of the Brothers, the ! They used to play in them. Them people been all over the wire. Just like Pusha Daddy. Do you hear those shoes?
Did they have any trombone solos in the brass band in those days?
Yeah, they're trombone solos.
Would he be featured on a funeral march? Well, yeah. Who was good at that?
Well, it was Sonny Allen. Albert Russo and Bill Madden. And Buddy Johnson. The trombone man.
It seems to me now that in the funeral marches, when the trombones have the lead or something, usually the two of them, they do that.
Yeah. Place the second. First and second together. That's pretty. It is. When they play together. Yeah. Right. 51 is good for that. 51, they really good number.
For the E record. What about E flat clarinet? Was there anybody special on the street there?
Right until Ed and Sherry. Ed and Sherry, he was like a white boy.
Well, he played with white bands too, I know. Oh yeah, he played with white bands. Dave Perkins or something.
Uh huh. He was called a doctor because his brother was a doctor. Uh huh.
Sherry you talking about?
Sherry? You know Dr. Sherry? I don't know him. But you heard talking.
I heard talking about when they got seen his office on drive. Yeah, well that's his brother.
Uh huh.
That's it.
And Johnny Dodds. Was a good E flat man too. Uh huh.
Who did he play with? Johnny Dodds.
Johnny Dodds. I didn't know I was playing regularly in the band, but they used to hire him, you know. I get it.
I used to like his playing on the records.
Good pleasure. Uh huh. His brother Baby could play some drums too.
Did he play much with the brass bands, Baby?
No. His Baby played much of it.
Do you remember what orchestras he played with?
No, I do not remember what orchestras he played with. But he played a long time ago. He lived up here.
Uh huh.
So.
I'm trying to remember where he and Johnny lived. Because I know they lived uptown.

Yeah, him and Johnny lived. Yeah, they lived on Tyler Downey Street. Up between I was in the Abbey. They had his sister. And they had a nephew and I playing clarinet. But he can play any better. He doubts himself.
Uh huh. He's a bully.
But he... He's a good player. Uh huh.
Sure.

If I could play clarinet like that boy, I would stick to clarinet. But he... He... He... He's a good player. And they can read good. But he don't think he can play enough. Shit. I got a match. Yeah. If I could play Clown-Ed like that boy, I would stick to Clown-Ed. He don't think he could play. But he doesn't know.
Well, I heard him with the Gibson band the other day. You know him, Lawrence Den? Oh, yeah. That's the one you're talking about, Lawrence Den?

Mm-hmm. I don't care about him much because he's got a big cab from there. He got a lot of cabs. And then he got that job, too. But we tried to get him in the Eureka band. Mm-hmm. We all went to the rehearsal and all. He didn't all come in. We played the music for him. I said, go ahead and ask the other one. He said, but I can make it. I said, I know you can make it.
They had two clarinets uptown with the Gibson the last time I saw them. Yeah. They had this fellow, they call him Red Dog Franklin or something? Henry Dog.
Henry Dog.
Henry Dog, yeah.

Oh, Lord Henry Dog. Henry Dog. Henry Dog was in the corner. I said, though, Henry Dog has been in the corner way in my time. And I don't know who Henry Dog ever played better. He's in the spot about this. Just using the man that couldn't get enough part.

Henry Dog. Henry Dog. By the way, we were talking last time about the changes in drumming. Have there been many changes in drumming that you can describe how it happened? The changes in how? Well, I mean, in late years, the way they play drums now with these modern bands is different. And I wouldn't play drums.

I wouldn't play drums. Because the book will tell you that the best drum is your foundation. It's like this . It's like this . Honestly, you couldn't build this . It's like this . foundation. And the bass drum is a foundation of any band. And you gotta keep that bass drum going at all times. That hold that band together, you know. But the color playing drums now they hit. Open spaces and all that. And they'd be behind time sometimes, they'd be on time, on the side of time. And most of the drummers, they don't know what a drumstick is being. They just got to hit the cymbal. They keep on holding their hand. But they say, further, further, use them. Use them, use them. Them sticks gotta be hit. That's what they're for. Cause sometimes in music, I have played in music. You get out of the strings. Where the drum part, the boy says drums. It sticks. And you play so many boys with the sticks. And right down there next down, they say, brushes. When you draw them, you pick up your brushes. And then you play your brushes. One, then it comes back to sticks. And sometimes they say to make an eight. Well, you can make no eight with no brushes. And you can't make no 16 with a brush. And then you can make no 32nd, second of the brushes. And you can't make no 64th. The brushes, that's gotta be made with them sticks. And then where you get some music, where you got about six or eight or a row, you'll use stuff and you'll run and row to that bed. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. You tell them to roll drums. They can't roll. You tell somebody to make a grace note on drums. And a grace note is that there's no fear to make. That's it. Just like that. But you've got to do the mistakes to get the effect. You'll catch awesome waltzes. Waltzes are drumming guys that roll, playing waltzes. Waltzes. Just like that. You see that's your room. And then they got some music line. Where the drummer. Roll the band in. Was like the brass band. Was every piece we could see when the band was ready to play. I rode that band right on in there. See. I rode him in. And they'll come right on behind that rope. And they'll come up right. That's why I couldn't remember to play. That's the reason I wouldn't be bothered with my little boy. Because he had made me take a stick and knock his head out. He didn't want to play like they're playing today.
Charles.

Yeah. And I ain't for that kind of thing. If I couldn't teach him right now, I ain't going to teach him at all. But the first thing, if I was a kid, he couldn't help me. But that ain't how they go. And see, that would make me mad.

What would you play in the old style of drumming? Say, when you're starting out, what would you play on the first chords? Would you play on your snare or your cymbals or your wood blocks or your tom-toms or what?
The first chords. I'd play on my snare drum. You're a snare drum.
Now what would you play? Would you play off beat rolls or would you play rolls on the beat?
On the beat, sometimes on the beat, sometimes on the beat. And then I'd switch from that tune to the block.
I'd play that block.
I'd play that block a while. And I'd play that a while and I'd switch to something else. And then when I'd take a drum solo, I'd give everything out. See, I'd work all my stuff.
When did the drum solos come in? Did they play them in olden days?
Oh yeah, drum solos. A big, big, big drum solos. I helped the drummer play the solo. He wasn't a drummer. Yeah, I used to mix and turn solo.
What would you play going out?
Hmm?
What would you play going out on the last chord, I'd say?
On the cymbal and bass drum.
Would it be an olden cymbal or would you choke it with your hand or what?

Sometimes I'd choke it in the family. Well, seeing my cymbal, I'd start, I could hit it and grab my cymbal. Keep it on until I left. Oh, I had that pack with the fan. I put a drum stick here. And I'd wipe the drum stick with the thumb.
Underneath the cymbal there.
Yeah, kick it up. And I'd choke it with the ringer. You see, that would give it a different effect. It would give it from being open. And then sometimes men would be appetite not playing open.
Out in the open air. Out in the open air, you know. I guess you need to play loud with all that space around.
Oh yeah, it needs to play loud. And sometimes when a fan is soft, Bees and Weak going out soft, then I'd wipe the band on the cymbal and this thing with a stick. I'd clip each cymbal.
Not with a stick, no stick in your left hand. No stick in your left hand.
I'd choke it in your left hand. Just with your hand. I'd choke it with this hand and bees with this hand. See, I used to hit all kinds of raps. Wraps with this hand.
When did the band play soft and when did they play loud? At the beginning of the piece, would they play pretty loud or not?

Well, all pieces, you know. All music, your introduction should be heavy. And then you fall down the way and you hit that tree up. And play on down to the first ending. And then soft. And play on down to the second ending. And then go on up to the left hand corner. You're going out there. And you can go out screaming.
How much? Man, we've got so much I want to ask you. Well, when would you use your wood blocks? Hmm? When would you use your wood blocks?
Your music would tell you.
Your music would tell you?
Yeah, it's written on the music. It's wood block.
Well, suppose you were playing by head. Hmm? Suppose they were playing a head number, an entirely head.
Yeah, head number, you figure it out.
You just figure it out.

And when they were using car bells, you know when they had car bells. Yeah. The four car bells. Mm-hmm. Well, that was on the music too. And I used to play a hell of a car bells. Make a kangaroo noise.

Well, would you play car bells when the clarinet had the lead or would you play when the trumpet had the lead or the trombone or would it make any difference? The trumpet had the lead. Yeah. In those days, huh? No. Would they take down much, the trumpet players then? Yeah, yeah, they'd take down. Mm-hmm.
And then we had some, the name of the blocks. I've got a set of nine.
This is some of the blocks. How many of them would there be? Four blocks. Big round things?
It looked like apples.
Yeah, I know those things. Temple blocks? The temple blocks.
The temple blocks. Boy, when you get so you could play them temple blocks, that was pretty. Mm-hmm. They'd be playing soft, you know, and then you'd get warm. Or you'd get them four blocks.
Mm-hmm. Just like that.

So, it's the only one thing that was hard for me, like, whether it's Lydon or something, that thing, and I could play, but not good. We had one boy, Joe Sprott. He could show up that slide with him. It was pretty. They were like a trampoline. Mm-hmm.
I've seen Chinese play his.
Yeah, Chinese could play one, but he couldn't be like Joe Sprott. Joe Sprott was the best dad.
Did you make any records back in the old days? Was it in the 20s or so? Did I make any records? No. When did you make your first records?
When I made my first record, I would have went to Lydon.
Mm-hmm. Remember any of the tunes on the records? No. No. No. No. No.
No. We played for the governor. No. No. No.
No. No. No. No. No. No.

We played for the governor. We played for the governor every Saturday, for 13 weeks. And yeah, last year, during Christmas time, some man come and went to the Deputy Institute and he bought one of those old records. What's that thing made? And the Deputy Institute people called me up and told me to come down to the office. I know what them people want. Somebody had bought a record seller stand. And I was so surprised. And during the Christmas time, too. Mm-hmm .
Mm-hmm .
Mm-hmm . So, when Celestine made a record, every man playing on the record was his name was on
the record. Did you make any records with anybody besides Celestine?

No, I didn't make them, but I had a chance to make them, but I wouldn't have gone with them. The reason why I did make them, making records ain't easy enough. Oh, that ain't easy, yeah. I mean, everything's got to be right down the top. In that studio, you'd be shut up in that room so hot. And you don't talk, you won't wait by sign. Everything is signed with. Because they're basically something that comes out on the record. And then sometimes they'll make one number. You've got three or four records, four or five records. And they, today it had something on the tape and they cut that out. They put it together, they put it with the other stuff together to get the record. The record looked like they came with. And sometimes they put a song on record. They go like... You know what I made records? They didn't want you to imitate nobody. You have to play your own style. Yeah, don't imitate.
Well, something I forgot to ask you too, another thing. When you used to go up to Richard Taylor and play with Rene, you told me you bought a keg of beer at that time.
Oh, we used to buy it.
Were the kids drinking? Young kids in short pants and those days?

Sure, we used to get a keg of beer. They let one of the kids put down a quarter in the week. And sometimes we'd buy our ham. With that bread and salmon braises. Potato salad, hot dogs with buns. And after our reference of the Eason's Rick, they'd buy a bread and some time with the pig. They'd be putting red food and rice. And gumbo sometimes. And she'd really be eating every Sunday. With all the rain, you know.
They wouldn't let little boys drink then some beer, huh?
Oh, he's drinking inside.
I guess somebody's mom and daddy would be there to take care of you.
I don't know, but I know my name wasn't there. I will impress the people. Mm-hmm. All right.

Does that look like that's the end of it, Molly? Just about. Yeah, well, we better call it to a halt, because I know it's getting late in the day. We sure do thank you for doing this. We really appreciate it. Thank you.

segments.title: Opening of reel one, date and speakers
segments.summary: Names, date (April 1962) and speakers are established; Dick Allen returns to where they stopped, on Jesse Jackson's band.

segments.title: Jesse Jackson's Golden Leaf band and Arthur Williams
segments.summary: Happy says the band was the Golden Leaf with Jesse Jackson as manager; he lists members including Bud Russo, Lee Collins and clarinetist Arthur Williams, who is still alive.

segments.title: Band instrumentation: no piano, Tink, trombone
segments.summary: The band had no regular piano; they hired different players, often Tink. It had a trombone but no violin.

segments.title: Where the band played: dance halls and lawn parties
segments.summary: They played all over, in dance halls, at St. Elizabeth and St. Monica, and at the Royal Garden on Gravier Street.

segments.chapter: Tulane Brass Band and bass drum
segments.title: Starting out and joining Amos Raleigh's Tulane brass band
segments.summary: Happy describes the old band he began with and how Amos Raleigh picked him up for the Tulane brass band; the leader was a cornet player and father of Theodore Riley.

segments.chapter: Tulane Brass Band and bass drum
segments.title: Reading music in the brass band; clipping the part to the drum
segments.summary: The Tulane band read everything; Happy explains how a drummer clips the part to the rim of the drum.

segments.chapter: Tulane Brass Band and bass drum
segments.title: Ernest Rebennack teaches Happy bass drum in the Tuxedo band
segments.summary: Happy tells how Ernest, a reader, urged him to learn bass drum and how he later brought Little Jim into the Tuxedo band; Jim was close friends with Black Benny.

segments.chapter: Tulane Brass Band and bass drum
segments.title: Learning the bass drum by watching; Ernest's drum
segments.summary: Happy learned by watching and walking beside Ernest, tells of a parade where he outplayed him, and keeps Ernest's 24-inch bass drum.

segments.chapter: Tulane Brass Band and bass drum
segments.title: Tulane band personnel and brass-band instrumentation
segments.summary: Members of the Tulane band, and how brass bands of that era used E-flat and alto horns, baritone and bass, in eleven pieces.

segments.title: Tuxedo Brass Band roster when Happy joined
segments.summary: Happy lists members of the Tuxedo band, including Shots, the Pajot, Russo, Sonny and old man Tats; he played snare, then moved to bass drum.

segments.title: Tuxedo band and Louis Armstrong's departure
segments.summary: Asked whether he joined the Tuxedo before or after Louis Armstrong, Happy says shortly after, and played jobs with him.

segments.title: Celestin's nicknames
segments.summary: Talk of the many nicknames of Celestin, including Papa, Oscar, Dog and Nostrils, and how he did not mind them.

segments.chapter: Tulane Brass Band and bass drum
segments.title: What the Tulane band played and who was in it
segments.summary: The Tulane band was unrelated to the Tulane Club though it played for it; it did funerals, parades and dances with mostly uptown players.

segments.title: Tuning snare and bass drums
segments.summary: Happy explains what sharp and flat snare drums mean, tuning by ear, tuning the bass drum to G, and tom-toms.

segments.title: The boyhood band with Louis Armstrong, Richard Taylor and Joe Rene
segments.summary: Happy was born in 1894 and was a little older than Armstrong; the boys in short pants rehearsed at a grocery.

segments.title: Richard Taylor's instruments and George Washington on bass
segments.summary: Taylor bought many instruments but could not play; George Washington played upright bass in the boys' band as well as trombone.

segments.title: Short pants and long pants for young musicians
segments.summary: Boys wore short pants until about sixteen to eighteen; Happy had learned his instrument before going out.

segments.title: Teacher David Jones and wrist technique
segments.summary: David Jones taught him to read; the rolls he picked up himself, playing from the wrist.

segments.title: Second-lining and watching drummers J.D. Chandler and another
segments.summary: As a boy Happy second-lined behind two hard-drinking drummers, including J.D. Chandler, who played in the Pacific brass band.

segments.title: Playing with Punch, then Ridgley's Tuxedo and the split with Celestin
segments.summary: After Jesse Jackson Happy played with Kid Punch, then Ridgley's Tuxedo; the falling-out between Ridgley and Celestin led to two Tuxedo bands.

segments.title: The contest between Ridgley's and Celestin's bands
segments.summary: Ridgley's band with David Jones and John Porter staged a publicized contest at the Pelican against Celestin's band, judged by professors.

segments.title: Celestin recruits Happy; 28 years in his band
segments.summary: When Celestin's drummer failed to show, Happy filled in and was talked into joining; he stayed 28 years, travelling.

segments.title: Belmatt and hardships on the road
segments.summary: Belmatt, also a drummer, and the road hardships with second-hand cars and playing dances.

segments.title: Identifying the photo of Ridgley's band; opening the Pelican
segments.summary: Looking at a photograph, Happy names Emma Barrett, Joe Watson, Shots, Alex Scott, Miner and Robert Hall, and their instruments.

segments.title: Joe Watson, E-flat clarinet and Sam Morgan
segments.summary: Joe Watson played clarinet and sax and was a good E-flat player; he played with Sam Morgan after Ridgley.

segments.title: Kid Rene leads the boys' band; the first parade, a carnival job for $3.50
segments.summary: Happy's first parade was a carnival day for three and a half dollars, a good wage.

segments.title: The Rene kids' brass band repertoire and Rene's playing
segments.summary: The Tulane played patriotic marches by hand; Rene's kids played juke music; Rene was a sweet cornet player but afraid to travel.

segments.title: Playing in Tom Albert's string band
segments.summary: Happy played in Tom Albert's string band, who drank his own whiskey, with banjo, clarinet by John Handy and a bass player named Jake.

segments.title: George Washington and Louis Armstrong's early work
segments.summary: George Washington played with Bud Petit and Chris Kelly; Armstrong played with everybody before settling at Tom Anderson's.

segments.title: Clay Jones's big bass drum and cymbal
segments.summary: Trumpeters helped young drummers; Happy describes Clay Jones's very large bass drum played with a cymbal in the other hand.

segments.title: How Happy got his nickname; other Happys
segments.summary: A girl first called him Happy; he became Black Happy, with Red Hat; Remus Matthew was another Happy.

segments.title: Birthplace, Dave Perkins and neighborhood parades
segments.summary: Happy was born on Dryades between Washington and Sixth; Dave Perkins lived nearby, and neighborhood parades were many.

segments.title: Blind pianist Rosebud and Clarence Williams at Big Du Bois
segments.summary: A blind teacher, Rosebud, played piano at Big Du Bois's tonk, near Howard Avenue; Dick asks about his era.

segments.title: Boogie woogie and George Thomas
segments.summary: Brief talk about when boogie woogie began in New Orleans and the number Hopscotch Blues.

segments.chapter: Jack Carey, Red Allen and repertoire
segments.title: Jack Carey's band, Punch and Red Allen
segments.summary: Happy played with Jack Carey with Punch; Red Allen was a young boy then.

segments.chapter: Jack Carey, Red Allen and repertoire
segments.title: Old Man Allen's band and Happy playing bass drum for him
segments.summary: Old Man Allen's brass band, his hard music, his cap, and Happy playing bass drum for him.

segments.chapter: Jack Carey, Red Allen and repertoire
segments.title: Allen's unlucky cap and his hard brass-band music
segments.summary: Happy tells of Allen's cap, the good times together, and the hard music he brought to his band.

segments.chapter: Jack Carey, Red Allen and repertoire
segments.title: Who was in Jack Carey's band
segments.summary: Happy lists Jack Carey's band members and his habit of hiring extra players.

segments.chapter: Jack Carey, Red Allen and repertoire
segments.title: Old repertoire: blues, quadrilles, head numbers
segments.summary: Early bands made up their own tunes; the quadrille was going out when Happy started, and chardises were played by head.

segments.title: Funeral marches and old band music
segments.summary: There are many funeral marches played by head; bands cut names off music to stop others copying.

segments.title: Favorite street players; John Porter and David Jones
segments.summary: Favorite men were from the Tuxedo, Onward and Tourist bands; John Porter on baritone solos and David Jones's background.

segments.title: Trombone solos in funeral marches
segments.summary: Sonny Allen, Albert Russo, Bill Madden and Buddy Johnson were good trombone soloists.

segments.title: E-flat clarinet players: Eddie Sherry, Johnny Dodds, Baby Dodds and others
segments.summary: Eddie Sherry, Johnny Dodds and Baby Dodds are remembered; later talk of clarinetists with the Eureka and Gibson bands, Henry Dog.

segments.title: Changes in modern drumming
segments.summary: Happy criticizes modern drummers who neglect sticks and rolls and says he would not teach his boy that way.

segments.title: Old-style snare, solos, cymbal choking and dynamics
segments.summary: Happy explains playing snare, block and rolls, drum solos, choking the cymbal, and band dynamics.

segments.title: Wood blocks, car bells, temple blocks and Joe Sprott
segments.summary: When wood blocks and car bells were used, temple blocks, and Joe Sprott as the best on them.

segments.title: Making records and playing for the governor
segments.summary: Happy remembers few recordings, played for the governor, and describes how hard studio work was.

segments.title: Kegs of beer and Sunday meals with the boys' band
segments.summary: Boys in the first band bought beer and Sunday food with weekly quarters.

segments.title: Closing of the interview
segments.summary: Dick Allen thanks Happy and ends the session.
